==Problem 17==
In a race among <imath>5</imath> snails, there is at most one tie, but that tie can involve any number of snails. For example, the result might be that Dazzler is first; Abby, Cyrus, and Elroy are tied for second; and Bruna is fifth. How many different results of the race are possible?

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 180 \qquad\textbf{(B) } 361 \qquad\textbf{(C) } 420 \qquad\textbf{(D) } 431 \qquad\textbf{(E) } 720</imath>

==Solution 1==
Intuitive solution:
We perform casework based on how many snails tie. Let's say we're dealing with the following snails: <imath>A,B,C,D,E</imath>.

<imath>5</imath> snails tied: All <imath>5</imath> snails tied for <imath>1</imath>st place, so only <imath>1</imath> way.

<imath>4</imath> snails tied: <imath>A,B,C,D</imath> all tied, and <imath>E</imath> either got <imath>1</imath>st or last. <imath>{5}\choose{1}</imath> ways to choose who isn't involved in the tie and <imath>2</imath> ways to choose if that snail gets first or last, so <imath>10</imath> ways.

<imath>3</imath> snails tied: We have <imath>ABC, D, E</imath>. There are <imath>3! = 6</imath> ways to determine the ranking of the <imath>3</imath> groups. There are <imath>5\choose2</imath> ways to determine the two snails not involved in the tie. So <imath>6 \cdot 10 = 60</imath> ways.

<imath>2</imath> snails tied: We have <imath>AB, C, D, E</imath>. There are <imath>4! = 24</imath> ways to determine the ranking of the <imath>4</imath> groups. There are <imath>5\choose{3}</imath> ways to determine the three snails not involved in the tie. So <imath>24 \cdot 10 = 240</imath> ways.

<imath>1</imath> snail tied: This is basically just every snail for a place, so <imath>5! = 120</imath> ways.

The answer is <imath>1+10+60+240+120 = \boxed{\text{(D) }431}</imath>.

~lprado

==Solution 2==
Split the problem into cases. A tie of <imath>n</imath> snails has <imath>\dbinom{5}{n}</imath> ways to choose the snails that are tied, <imath>6-n</imath> ways to choose which place they tie for, and <imath>(5-n)!</imath> to place the remaining snails.

1. No tie <imath>\implies5!=120</imath>

2. Tie of 2 snails <imath>\implies\dbinom{5}{2}\cdot4\cdot3!=240</imath>

3. Tie of 3 snails <imath>\implies\dbinom{5}{3}\cdot3\cdot2!=60</imath>

4. Tie of 4 snails <imath>\implies\dbinom{5}{4}\cdot2=10</imath>

5. Tie of all 5 snails <imath>\implies1</imath>

The answer is <imath>120+240+60+10+1=\boxed{\text{(D) }431}</imath> ~Tacos_are_yummy_1

==Solution 3 (Answer Choice Reasoning)==
For the case of a 5-way tie, we have <imath>\dbinom{5}{5}=1</imath> cases. We can assume this leads to an answer that ends in 1, leaving only <imath>B</imath> and <imath>D</imath>. By just accounting for the cases for a 1-way tie (<imath>5!=120</imath>) and 2-way tie (<imath>\dbinom{5}{2}\cdot4\cdot3!=240</imath>), it immediately shows that <imath>B</imath> does not work. Therefore, the answer is <imath>\boxed{\text{(D) }431}</imath>
~shreyan.chethan, cleaned up by cweu001, vintage_god

Notice that with 2 remaining choices, through guessing, the expected value of your points is <imath>\frac{6}{2}=3</imath>, and not answering gives 1.5 points. Therefore, you gain an expected value of <imath>1.5</imath> points by answering. It would be best to always guess whenever you can get rid of <imath>2</imath> or more answers. If you can only eliminate <imath>1</imath> answer, not guessing will give you <imath>1.5</imath> points, but guessing also gives you an expected value of <imath>1.5</imath> points. I usually leave it blank if I can only get rid of <imath>1</imath> answer choice.
~shreyan.chethan, edited by BenjaminDong01, added by PerseverePlayer , and added by Aarav22

Sidenote : Usually, you should aim to look at the closer option choices than the extreme ones.

==Solution 4 (Rigorous Solution 1; same logic)==

Call the snails <imath>A,B,C,D,E</imath> in said order apart of the set <imath>S</imath>, and define <imath>S_{T}</imath> to be the set of ties regarding <imath>T</imath> snails. Define a '''maxima tie''' to be a set <imath>\mathcal{M}</imath> that retains a tie between <imath>k</imath> members for <imath>2 \le k \le 5</imath>. Consider casework on all '''maxima ties'''.

If no '''maxima ties''' exist, then the problem degenerates into how many word rearrangements exist for <imath>ABCDE</imath>, which is <imath>5! = 120</imath>.

If <imath>k=2</imath> '''maxima tie''' exist, then note that if the tie is held between <imath>A,B</imath>, it is the same as a tie holding for <imath>B,A</imath>, meaning we have <imath>\frac{5 \cdot 4}{2} = 10</imath> ways to choose our '''maxima tie'''. Then, the word rearrangement for <imath>\mathcal{M}CDE</imath> is <imath>4! = 24</imath>, yielding 240 cases.

If <imath>k=3</imath> '''maxima tie''' exist, then note that if a tie is held between <imath>A,B,C</imath>, it is the same for the other 5 iterations. Out of one iteration, 5 other copies exist that yield the same result, meaning our cases for the '''maxima tie''' are <imath>\frac{5 \cdot 4 \cdot 3}{6} = 10</imath>. Then, the word rearrangement for <imath>\mathcal{M}DE</imath> is <imath>3! = 6</imath>, yielding 60 cases.

If <imath>k=4</imath> '''maxima tie''' exist, then every partition of <imath>A,B,C,D</imath> yields 23 other copies, meaning there are 5 acknowledgeable cases. Then the word rearrangement for <imath>\mathcal{M}E</imath> is <imath>2! = 2</imath>, yielding 10 cases.

If <imath>k=5</imath> '''maxima tie''' exist, then every partition of <imath>A,B,C,D,E</imath> yields 119 other copies, meaning there is only one acknowledgeable case. Then, the word rearrangement for <imath>\mathcal{M}</imath> is <imath>1! = 1</imath> yielding 1 case.

The desired answer is then

<cmath>120 + \sum_{T = k \neq {1} \in S_{T}} \textbf{maxima tie plausible cases}</cmath>
<cmath>120 + 240 + 60 + 10 + 1 = \boxed{431}</cmath>

~Pinotation
